text: Good evening. I'm Pilar Ochoa, and I run the programs at the San José parish hall: the food pantry on Saturdays, and the Tuesday citizenship class we hold with the library across Grand. Last month eleven of our students passed. $ [worried] I want to say something about what is coming out of Washington. These policies are divisive. They split a town into people who come to class and people who stay home, into families who answer the door and families who don't. Four of my students stopped coming this month, not because they did anything, but because they were afraid of a sign-in sheet. $ [warm] This neighbourhood works because people cross Grand in both directions. Half the young people in this room translate for their parents. That is not a problem to fix. It is the best thing we have.

_to the moderator_ What would I ask of the next governor? Two things. First, interpreters in every clinic and city office, in person when it matters, so nobody signs a paper they can't read. I sit with a lady at the clinic every other Thursday so she can tell the doctor the truth. That shouldn't depend on me. Second, fund the places where people meet each other: the library nights, the know-your-rights clinics, the class. Not one community's room. The doors between the rooms. $ [warm] And say it out loud, as one state: the people Washington is pointing at are our neighbours. They pay the taxes, they carry the boxes at the pantry, they coach the soccer. Stand next to them in public. People here are watching who stands where.

Good evening. I'm Pilar Ochoa, from the San José parish hall: the pantry, the roof raffle, and the Tuesday citizenship class we run with the library across Grand. Last month eleven of our students passed. $ I'll be honest, this has been a good year to do this work. When the president says this country is better for having people from everywhere, my students hear it. The city called to fund the class. The schools send their letters in two languages, side by side, on the same page. That is progress, and I want to say thank you for it out loud. $ But a good speech in Washington doesn't walk a grandmother into the clinic. People do that. The young people in this room who speak two languages do it every day, and they should be proud of it.

_to the moderator_ What should the next governor do? Build on it while the wind is with us. Fund interpreters in the clinics for good, not as a pilot that ends in June. Put money into the programs that bring people together: the library nights, the citizenship class, the block-party potluck, the soccer league where half the parents yell in Spanish and half in English. $ [warm] And make it easy for every community to join in, not only mine. Invite the Club Jerez, invite the Chamber, invite the people who never come to meetings like this one. A state with many cultures is stronger when they know each other's names. I would like the next governor to learn a few of ours.
Both doors, every question. You sound like somebody who should be helping me run the Tuesday class.
You'd send everyone straight across Grand. Fine. I'd only ask you not to lock the door behind them.
You'd keep each of us in our own room. I understand why. I just think the room gets smaller every year that way.
You listened more than you answered. That's fair. Come on Tuesday and tell me what you heard.
A little of everything, like most of this neighbourhood. Thank you for getting up there, {playerName}.
